description: We are a Milan-based team of six students spanning Aerospace and Electronic Engineering (Politecnico di Milano), Physics and Computer Science (University of Milano-Bicocca), and Economics (Bocconi University). Combining physics-based differential modeling, multi-scale NASA Earth observation pipelines, software engineering, and agricultural economics, we built FIELDWISE to help farmers adapt multi-year crop rotations to a shifting climate
summary: Farmers must choose crop rotations while balancing production, resource use and economic returns under uncertain conditions. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, FIELDWISE is a decision-support prototype that makes these trade-offs easier to assess. At a pilot location in Cremona, northern Italy, it combines NASA POWER weather data, soil information and published agronomic parameters to simulate maize, soybean and soft wheat sequences with optional rye cover crops. A daily model tracks crop development, water and nitrogen balances, and humus dynamics under three irrigation scenarios and historical weather from 2000 to 2022. Alternatives are compared through user-weighted indicators of yield, historical downside performance, resource requirements, soil outcomes and an annualized partial economic margin. Evaluation against satellite observations and provincial statistics supports selected model responses: simulated maize yields correlate with detrended provincial yields at r = 0.70 under capped irrigation, while soybean results are inconclusive and wheat yields show a negative correlation. Sensitivity analysis shows uncertainty in the ranking of alternatives. FIELDWISE offers a structured basis for exploring rotations, with potential value in reducing evaluation effort. Its practical benefits depend on further validation, farm-specific feasibility checks and integration into agricultural advisory services.

FIELDWISE — Know your land. Grow your future.

What it does

FIELDWISE is a decision-support prototype that helps farmers compare crop rotations on their own field. The user selects a field on an interactive map, enters the current rotation and the irrigation available, and chooses what matters most: yield, performance in bad years, irrigation, fertilizer, soil health or economic margin. FIELDWISE then compares the current rotation with every alternative and explains, in real units and plain language, what changing would gain and what it would risk.

It does not declare a universally "best" rotation. It makes the trade-offs visible, so that the final decision stays with farmers and agronomists.

Our pilot is the Po Valley near Cremona, Italy, one of Europe's most intensive maize areas. Many farms there grow maize after maize, which depletes soil organic matter, increases nitrogen losses to groundwater and raises exposure to drought and heat.

How it works

At its core is a daily simulation engine written in Python. For every day it computes three linked balances:

  • Water, with the FAO-56 dual crop coefficient method: Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, soil evaporation, crop transpiration, water stress, Curve Number runoff, deep percolation and irrigation within the chosen water limit.
  • Nitrogen: mineralization of soil organic matter, crop uptake linked to transpiration, fertilizer, biological fixation by soybean, release from residues, and nitrate leaching.
  • Soil organic matter, with the Hénin-Dupuis humus balance: inputs from crop residues and cover crops, minus mineralization.

Crop development follows growing degree days. Yield is limited by water stress (FAO-33 yield response), heat stress at flowering and the penalty for repeating the same crop.

The key design choice is that the soil remembers. Water, mineral nitrogen, residues and humus carry over from one day to the next and from one crop to the next, so the order of crops matters, not only their choice.

Historical weather, not forecasts. FIELDWISE does not predict next season. It replays real weather from NASA POWER: 2000–2022 at the pilot, quality-checked against ground stations, giving 17 historical starting years after a warm-up cycle. All 216 three-year combinations of maize, soybean and soft wheat, with or without a rye cover crop, are simulated from every starting year under three water scenarios: rainfed, capped irrigation and unrestricted irrigation. That is 11,016 simulations for the pilot field, computed in about 6 seconds. Equivalent rotations are then merged into 45 distinct classes per irrigation scenario. Risk is the spread across real years, including droughts such as 2003 and 2022.

Explainable comparison. Each rotation is described by indicators in real units:

  • median yield and worst-year yield;
  • irrigation (mm/year);
  • nitrogen fertilizer and nitrogen leached (kg N/ha/year);
  • change in soil humus;
  • a modelled partial economic margin (€/ha/year);
  • compliance with encoded regional integrated-production rules.

Farmer priorities enter only at the end, as transparent weights. A Pareto front shows the options that no other alternative beats on every indicator. Reports explain evidence and risks for each alternative and can be exported as PDF and Excel.

Experimental extensions

  • Longer-term optimization. A Beam Search optimizer explores three successive three-crop rotations (nominally nine years) for yield, margin or cost. It carries the simulated soil state from one cycle to the next and prunes options that break the encoded rules.
  • Climate stress tests. Monthly delta changes in temperature, rainfall, radiation and humidity are applied to the historical NASA POWER record for several horizons and emissions scenarios. Reference evapotranspiration is recomputed with Penman-Monteith. The deltas are currently illustrative assumptions in the range of CMIP6-type projections, not yet derived from downscaled model output. These are conditional "what if" scenarios, not forecasts.

Use of NASA data

  • NASA POWER daily weather drives every simulation.
  • SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI, ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration and GPM IMERG precipitation are used to test the model, not to tune it.

We also use ISRIC SoilGrids for soil properties, ARPA Lombardia ground stations and ERSAF soil data for quality checks, and ISTAT provincial yields for validation.

Validation and honesty

We tested the model against independent observations at the Cremona pilot and report the results as they are.

  • SMAP: simulated soil-moisture anomalies follow SMAP with a correlation of about 0.70.
  • MODIS: simulated maize water stress follows MODIS NDVI with 0.60.
  • ISTAT: simulated maize yields follow detrended provincial yields with 0.70 under capped irrigation.
  • ECOSTRESS: the seasonal cycle of evapotranspiration is reproduced (0.77), but the model overestimates it by about 1.6 mm/day in the growing season under capped irrigation.
  • Weak or untested: soybean yield results are inconclusive, the wheat yield correlation is negative, and nitrogen and humus processes are not independently validated at field scale.
  • Sensitivity: when all uncertain parameters are varied together, the top-ranked rotation stays first in about 12–30% of cases, depending on the water scenario.

This is why FIELDWISE presents comparisons and uncertainty notes rather than prescriptions.

Every parameter is stored with its source (FAO manuals, Italian regional regulations, peer-reviewed literature) or flagged as a declared assumption and tested in the sensitivity analysis.

What makes it creative

  • A time machine for the field. It answers "what would have happened on my land over the last twenty years if I had farmed differently?", using real NASA weather instead of a forecast.
  • Rotations as sequences. Most tools evaluate one crop in one season. FIELDWISE evaluates the sequence, with a soil that carries its history.
  • Satellites as referees. NASA observations are used to check the model, and the interface states openly where it is reliable and where it is not.

Tools and technologies

  • Engine: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Numba), with parameters in documented YAML files.
  • API: FastAPI, with background jobs for data preparation and the Beam Search.
  • Web app: Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript, with MapLibre GL and Terra Draw for drawing fields.
  • Exports: PDF reports with ReportLab, plus Excel export.
  • Tests: an automated test suite (pytest), including a reproduction of the FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration example.
  • Data caching: cached data record their source, download date and checksum, so analyses can be reproduced.

Limitations and next steps

  • Scope. FIELDWISE is a research prototype. Validation is concentrated on the Cremona pilot. Each field is represented by a single point, and the weather comes from a NASA POWER grid cell of about 50 km.
  • Economics. The economic output is a partial margin, not total farm profit.
  • Hosted demo. Data preparation for a new field can be slow on hosted infrastructure.

Next steps:

  • deltas derived from NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 model output for the climate module;
  • independent field validation with farm data;
  • more crops;
  • faster data preparation.
